items.title: macOS Tahoe 26.7 beta references several unreleased products like Home Hub
items.content_html:
Apple inadvertently left a lot of feature flags visible in its macOS Tahoe 26.7 release candidate, which include references to products like AirPods with cameras, the OLED iPad mini, and more.

Developer betas are one of the easiest ways for Apple to accidentally share future product information. It has occurred before, like during iOS 26 testing, and has happened again on Monday.

According to information discovered by MacRumors in the macOS Tahoe 26.7 release candidate, Apple has many new products in development. Some are known from previous leaks, while others have designators that can't be tied to any other product.

The various product identifiers reference products like a future Apple Vision Pro and Home Hub product. There are also references to Apple Intelligence in China and the upcoming foldable iPhone that some call "iPhone Ultra."

The following product identifiers are referenced in the macOS Tahoe 26.7 release candidate:

Apple Home

  • J490 & J491: Home Hub, speaker base and wall mounted variety, respectively
  • B525: next-generation HomePod mini with something called "Argentium" installed
  • J229: Possibly Apple's security camera

There are also references to "Pebble," which has been previously reported as the codename for Apple's rumored homeOS platform.

Other tidbits include colors like rose, pink, silver, space gray, and starlight. These could be used for a product like the next-generation HomePod mini.

HomeAAccessory17,2 and HomeAccessory17,3 were also spotted, though it isn't clear what these products might be. A mention of "audio_accessory_visual_reasoning" code string was also found, which could be used by a Home Hub with a camera.

Headphones

  • B790: AirPods with cameras that are expected later in 2026, includes reference to "B790 start image stream failed for left bud"
  • B518 & B522: Possible upcoming Beats headphones

Code also mentions AirPodsPro1,4, which would reference a fourth-generation AirPods Pro. There is also a reference to AirPod3,5.

iPhone

  • V62: iPhone Air 2 due in the spring
  • V63: iPhone 18 Pro
  • V64: iPhone 18 Pro Max
  • V67: iPhone 18 due in the spring
  • V68: Apple's foldable iPhone

Mac

  • J804: MacBook Pro with M6
  • J833 & J834: next-generation iMac
  • K114c, K114s, K116c, & K116s: Possible MacBook Pro models with OLED

Other products

  • J510 & J511: next-generation iPad mini with OLED and A19 Pro
  • N109: next-generation Apple Vision Pro

An updated Apple TV remote was also referenced with ATVRemote1,5. A new Apple TV could be revealed at any time with an updated remote.

There are also a ton of product identifiers that don't have an obvious product tied to them. They are:

  • A3436, A3437, A3438, A3439, A3440, A3441
  • A3456, A3457
  • A3465
  • A3529, A3530, A3531, A3532, A3533
  • A3543
  • A3577
  • Device1,8234
  • Device1,8236
  • Device1,8238
  • Device1,8240
  • Device1,8241
  • Device1,8242
  • Device1,8246
  • Device1,8247
  • Device1,8248

These were found in feature flags that should have been turned off before publishing the macOS Tahoe 26.7 release candidate. Mistakes do happen, and while this isn't too critical of a leak, it is still quite the insight into Apple's upcoming product release cycle.

items.title: Amazon joins the list of companies destroying rare books to feed to the AI machine
items.content_html:
An AirTag hidden in a rare book followed its journey to a Las Vegas warehouse, where it was likely destroyed in an effort to supply fresh data to hungry LLMs.

I don't know if you've noticed, but everything is becoming increasingly AI-generated. Whether it's news, music, or social media, AI has seemingly stuck all of its nasty little fingers into any pie it can find.

Experts have long warned that eventually we'd get to the point where AI was training itself on data that AI had created, and we're pretty sure that point is behind us. And that's not actually particularly useful, it turns out.

It's harder to pass the Turing test when everything sounds exactly like it fell out of the back of a ChatGPT prompt. And that's why AI companies don't really want the AI version of the human centipede.

They want to train AI off of human-produced content. Which, as a human who produces human-produced content, you'd assume I'd be relieved to hear that I at least have a spot in the pipeline.

items.title: iPhone Ultra screen protectors have asymmetric corners
items.content_html:
A leaker with a decent track record has shown what is claimed to be a screen protector for the forthcoming iPhone Ultra, and it shows the device's unusual corners.

In June 2026, leaker Ice Universe showed off what was purported to be a prototype of the iPhone Ultra. Now the same leaker is back with an image of a screen protector accessory, which appears to back up claims of the device's shape.

That's significant because for the first time, Apple is reportedly designing an iPhone that does not have a uniform shape. Instead, it will be straight on the side that holds the hinge, then have more of a curve to the opposite side.

This is the screen protector for the iPhone Ultra. You can see, the iPhone Ultra actually has an irregular screen with one side square and the other round. Oh my God, can you even handle that? pic.twitter.com/qpQHZHiqcD

— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) August 11, 2026

In a subsequent post, the leaker claimed that the protector is really intended to cover the entire glass area rather than solely the display. It's not impossible that Apple will give the display rounded corners on one side, but there wouldn't seem to be any advantage to doing that.

I'm sure this is just a misunderstanding - the protective film covers the entire glass panel, not exactly the same as the actual screen display area. The iPhone Ultra screen itself is still a symmetrical rounded rectangle. pic.twitter.com/Iwu52050uw

— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) August 11, 2026

One of the leaked images also shows a camera cutout. It's a single cutout placed toward the top right of the screen, and will be for the front or selfie camera.

The iPhone Ultra is to be Apple's first folding iPhone. It's expected to be launched in September 2026, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

items.title: Apple TV drops trailer and launch date for Australian thriller 'Last Seen'
items.content_html:
Apple TV has released the first trailer for "Last Seen," its upcoming thriller starring Patrick Brammall, ahead of the series premiere on September 9.

In "Last Seen," police detective Ian Ridley's daughter vanished 11 years ago without a trace. Then, a distress call from a teenage girl convinces Ridley she may be Maggie and renews his search for his daughter.

The series is based on CWA John Creasey Dagger Award-winning author Ryan David Jahn's book, "The Dispatcher." The first two episodes will premiere on Wednesday, September 9, and new episodes will release Wednesday through October 7.

Apple TV also shared a two-minute trailer for the series on its YouTube channel.

It stars Gotham Award winner Patrick Brammall as Ridley. Alongside Brammall, the cast includes Brendan Cowell, Daniel Henshall, Chloe Jean Lourdes, Zahra Newman, Maxine Peake, and Jessica Wren.

"Last Seen" was entirely filmed in Victoria, Australia, with Kris Mrksa adapting the novel and serving as an executive producer. Emmy Award-nominated filmmaker Christian Schwochow directed and executive produced the series.

"Last Seen" joins Apple's ever-expanding lineup of thrillers. That includes well-known titles like the workplace psychological thriller "Severance," which Apple recently acquired in a $70 million ownership transfer.

items.title: iPhone 20 Pro will be bigger with familiar aspect ratios, be bezel free
items.content_html:
The iPhone 20 Pro display will be the same aspect ratio as previous models, while still being slightly bigger. Combined with the glass cover, it should result in a bezel-less effect in the final version.

Apple's anniversary smartphone, the often-rumored iPhone 20 Pro is believed to have both a glass-heavy design and much larger displays than usual. While the model is still far from becoming a reality, that hasn't stopped rumors from floating about it.

In the latest claim about the milestone release, Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station posted on Wednesday about the displays used in the iPhone 20 Pro series. Codenamed V73 and V74, the models are said to be bigger, but have the same aspect ratio as earlier Pro and Pro Max models.

This apparently means that Apple is going for a new bezel-less quad-curved design for the iPhone 20 Pro.

The leaker goes on to explain that the style of the smartphone will center around the use of a 2D flat screen with a glass cover. The cover will use optical refraction and be shaped to create a visual borderless effect.

We've heard this before...

Weibo leakers are not best known for their accuracy, though Digital Chat Station has a fairly reasonable track record among the usual suspects. That said, the leak isn't really bringing much new to the table.

On August 4, the account posted about Apple prototyping two screen sizes, measuring 6.4 inches and 7 inches for the iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max. By comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6.3-inch screen and the Pro Max is 6.9 inches in size.

At the time, they also said that the aspect ratio would be maintained, and that a "bezel-less quad curved design" would be used.

The sizes weren't new either, as Digital Chat Station also talked about them on July 21. The use of a "four-micro-curve" OLED panel was also mentioned back in April by the account.

More recently, the glass usage was raised by fellow Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital, resurfacing previous rumors.

Arguably the biggest thing about Digital Chat Station's post is that it goes against a claim from an analyst that Apple cancelled its all-glass design for the iPhone 20.

items.title: Everyone at Apple is calling the foldable 'iPhone Ultra'
items.content_html:
A new rumor suggests that "everyone" at Apple calls the upcoming foldable iPhone the "iPhone Ultra," though that doesn't mean Apple will actually go with that name.

Apple keeps things like marketing names under a tight lock and key. It is rare, if ever, that the public learns about what something might be called before it is released.

However, you have to call the device something, and it seems a colloquial name has caught on internally at Apple. A social media post from Mark Gurman suggests that "everyone calls it the Ultra internally."

Everyone calls it the Ultra internally. We'll see what happens.

— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) August 11, 2026

The device has been referred to as the iPhone Fold here at AppleInsider, with an occasional dip into Ultra. The name is anyone's best guess at this point, and it seems highly unlikely that the true name is known by "everyone" at Apple.

Whether they are accidentally correct or talking openly about secret product names won't ever be known. But it won't be long before Apple finally reveals the product and we all get to learn the name first-hand.

Naming conventions aren't always predictable

Previous naming debates lasted right up until the product was revealed on stage. The iPhone Air was previously called "iPhone Slim" and the iPhone 16e was long believed to be an iPhone SE 4.

The iPhone Air name was also anyone's guess before it launched

The "Ultra" moniker has been used by Apple for its Apple Silicon chips most recently. However, that term is used to refer to the highest-end of a possible product, and that won't be the foldable iPhone in some respects.

Sure, Apple will put the best A-series chip it has in the foldable, and its display technology will be unmatched, but it may not be the "best" iPhone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max will still have a superior camera system, more rugged case, better battery life, and better cooling.

Until recently the iPhone lineup was a ladder you could climb up and down, but the iPhone Air added a branch so there are two pathways. The entry "e" model then the base model make up the bottom, then consumers choose between an iPhone Air and iPhone Pro.

The foldable iPhone will be above the Air in the lineup, not above the Pro. So, it is difficult to suggest that it would get the "Ultra" name.

Regardless, the folding iPhone will be the most expensive by far. Perhaps that will be enough to earn it the top-level moniker.

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Fold are expected to be revealed during an event in September. Whether or not the iPhone Fold will actually ship that month is another question entirely.

items.title: Apple Pay & Apple Card VP Jennifer Bailey is retiring
items.content_html:
The executive who spearheaded Apple Pay, Jennifer Bailey, is retiring after 12 years as Vice President of Internet Services and Apple Pay.

Under Bailey's leadership, Apple launched Apple Wallet, Apple Pay, and Apple Card. She also supervises Tap to Pay on iPhone, Apple Gift Cards, and Apple Cash internationally.

She joined the company in 2003 as Vice President of Worldwide Online Stores in 2003, and was promoted in 2014.

Bailey presently serves on the board of directors at PepsiCo. She was on the American Red Cross board from 2015 through 2024.

The departure was reported by Bloomberg on Tuesday afternoon. The venue cites a note to all employees penned by Eddy Cue.

The note in its entirety is below.

Under Jennifer's leadership, Apple Pay has changed the way hundreds of millions of our users pay, with a simpler, more secure, and private experience. She also led the development and growth of Apple Wallet, oversaw the development and launch of Apple Card, and led our work in Services fraud prevention and partner operations, Gift Cards, and Trust and Safety. And those are just a few of her achievements.

On a personal note, Jennifer has been an incredible friend and leader, and I will miss working with her.

Please join me in thanking Jennifer for her incredible contributions to Apple. Before Jennifer's transition at the end of October, we will announce our succession plan, and Jennifer will continue to be available to support the transition in an advisory role.

As we continue to work toward our vision of replacing the physical wallet, I'm more confident than ever in the work that we are all doing and look forward to an exciting future ahead.

Thank you,

Eddy

Also on the way out is Senior Director of Corporate Communications Josh Rosenstock. Rosenstock was hired away from Rolls-Royce in 2013, and has been in the role ever since.

I haven't spoken directly with Rosenstock in years, most notably during and after the Apple vs. Samsung trial. However, for over a decade, his emails to me and us were always a portent of something big.

Rosenstock's departure is routine. He is retiring as well.

attachments.title: Apple Pay & Apple Card VP Jennifer Bailey is retiring

items.title: iOS 27 celebrates your friends' birthdays with fireworks
items.content_html:
New in iOS 27 is a birthday reminder that means if you are on a call with someone, your iPhone will tell you if it's their special day with fireworks! The gift is still on you, though.

There may not be a smaller addition to iOS 27, but the Phone app's birthday reminder is a really nice touch. In the current betas, if you call someone, the Phone app checks the contact card you've got for them.

It does exactly the same if they call you, and it always has, as that's how it displays their name and probably a contact photo. But now it does one more thing.

If that contact card has their birthday, and if that's today, you'll get an unmissable notification about it whether you're calling them or they're calling you. Either way, unless you're really fast at putting the phone to your ear, you will see a birthday banner right there on your iPhone screen.

It's even animated, so that as the banner shows you that today is their birthday, it also has animated fireworks. You can't miss the banner and you can't miss the fireworks.

But that animation of fireworks can mean that you miss a detail. Apple's constant emphasis on privacy means that it won't even tell you a birthday without making sure you know how it knows.

Specifically, in the banner itself there will be a tiny note saying "Birthday - Found in Contacts." If you tap on that banner, you are taken through to the full Contacts card where, presumably, you can verify that the date is right.

Sweating the details

You can't really call this Apple Intelligence when it's just looking up the contact card of whoever you're talking to. But it is an example of the same thinking that makes Apple Intelligence useful.

That's because this is another case of Apple using the information you have on your device, and surfacing it to you when you need it. No passing your data to third-party firms, just making what you already have be more useful.

True, you could argue that you actually need a birthday reminder a little ahead of the day, in order to buy that gift. And if they're sitting there waiting for you to phone them on their birthday, you won't get this alert and now you're dead to them.

But still, it's a thoughtful addition and just another example of Apple thinking about people's use of iPhones rather than of the technological possibilities.

Thank you to AppleInsider reader Brae for reminding us about this!

attachments.title: iOS 27 celebrates your friends' birthdays with fireworks

items.title: Apple stocking up on OLED screens to offset RAM and SSD prices
items.content_html:
Apple's supply chain is now holding more iPhone OLED panels with Apple also ordering more of them, all to offset the growing cost of buying the components.

While the general effect of the ongoing memory price surge has resulted in more expensive components for suppliers, it also has other effects on the supply chain. In the case of Apple's iPhone production lines, there have been changes in the way they work.

According to sources cited by ETNews, Apple increased the display panel inventory holding period in the second quarter, from four weeks to six weeks. This refers to the average amount of time that a component will be kept in stock before it's used in production.

To a manufacturer, extending the period it holds onto components can increase the relative cost of storing it. There's also the benefit of being able to make bigger orders for components, potentially saving money by reducing the per-component cost due to the economies of scale.

A report source explained that the raw material prices to produce components have rapidly risen, alongside intense pricing pressures of other parts. The OLED panel inventory was therefore increased by Apple to stabilize prices.

An increase in orders

At the same time as increasing how long inventory is held for, Apple has also increased the size of its orders to match.

The second quarter is Apple's off-season for production, and usually has lower stockpiles of components until a rise before the September launch. This year, it's a bit different.

Display panel orders have apparently been higher than normal in Q2, in part because of the continued demand for the iPhone 17 series. Apple's global smartphone shipments increased 13% year-over-year.

The increase in orders is viewed as an attempt by Apple to minimize any rise in component cost by simply buying more of them in the first place. The larger the order, the lower the per-item cost to Apple.

Increasing orders and storing them for longer is a compromise, but one that minimizes how much of that extra cost gets handed down to consumers.

A continuing trend

While the report is about Apple's display issues, it's not the only part of its iPhone empire that has to deal with production issues.

Memory is a big and unavoidable problem. Manufacturing capacity in 2027 for the major vendors is already allocated ahead of time, as customers fight to secure a supply for their products.

The cost of memory has even led to supply chain rumors claiming TSMC has a billion-dollar stockpile of Apple chips it can't complete, due to not having enough memory to complete packaging.

While that particular rumor is probably fake, it does show that the memory crisis goes far beyond increasing the price of one important component.

attachments.title: Apple stocking up on OLED screens to offset RAM and SSD prices

items.title: First hints emerge about how much extra Apple Intelligence features will cost
items.content_html:
Apple CEO Tim Cook said that there would be costs for some Apple Intelligence features, and iCloud+ tier limits on HomeKit Secure Video have popped up in the latest iOS 27 beta.

On August 10, Apple released the fifth developer beta for its fall operating system updates. However, it seems the beta has hinted that there will be some changes to the way Apple prices iCloud+ for upper-tier users.

One of the current benefits for iCloud+ is HomeKit Secure Video. The base 50GB plan includes HomeKit Secure Video support for one camera, with the 200GB package supporting 5, according to Apple's support page at the time of publication.

The upper tiers of iCloud+, with 2TB to 12TB of capacity, currently include support for an unlimited number of cameras under HomeKit Secure Video.

However, Monday's fifth developer beta for iOS 27 includes some text when checking your HomeKit Secure Camera settings. Screenshots from Apple Home Authority on X when using the 2TB plan lists the user as supporting just five cameras.

Under the existing subscription model, the 2TB account should have unlimited cameras, not five. A plausible answer here is that the limits are being applied wrong in the app, and could be corrected later.

Interesting change in iOS 27 Beta 5 for Apple Home

Apple now shows exactly how many HomeKit Secure Video cameras your iCloud+ plan supports, along with which Apple Intelligence camera features are included.

But there's something strange going on.

I'm already on the 2TB pic.twitter.com/tplFxYZzBp

— Apple Home Authority (@helloapplehome) August 10, 2026

Another screenshot from Stephen Robles shows text stating "Your iCloud+ plan includes video summaries for 15 cameras." Robles claims he is using the highest iCloud plan, which would cost $59.99 per month for 12TB of capacity.

The limitation of 15 cameras is not any of the options Apple states in the support page.

Apple has not yet indicated changes to iCloud+ are inbound, and its support pages also don't mention any upcoming alterations.

While this could be a bug of some form in the iOS 27 developer beta, it could just as easily be Apple revising what it offers its customers.

attachments.title: First hints emerge about how much extra Apple Intelligence features will cost

items.title: iCloud Private Relay failures manifest a new class-action lawsuit against Apple
items.content_html:
Apple is now facing an inevitable class action lawsuit over a flaw in iCloud Private Relay that exposes a user's identity. It's a lawsuit from the same firm that got a $250M settlement over Siri AI's delays.

Any Apple security issue that surfaces is a potential lawsuit target, and can quickly be seized upon by law firms smelling an opportunity. Once again, that has happened to Apple in the wake of stories about iCloud Private Relay.

The Clarkson Law Firm has filed an attempted class action lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of deceiving consumers with its marketing of iCloud+ subscriptions. Specifically, for perceived failures in iCloud Private Relay.

Readers may be aware of Clarkson Law Firm from the settlement with Apple over the delayed introduction of Siri AI. While the class-action lawsuit was settled in December 2025, it wasn't until May 2026 that the $250M settlement details were actually revealed.

Under the new lawsuit, 9to5Mac writes that the firm is going after what it calls an "outrageous betrayal of consumer trust." Apple customers paid based on a promise of privacy, the firm insists, which was broken after a few years.

The protection of iCloud Private Relay "simply didn't work," the firm continued, exposing consumers to potentially being tracked and profiled in ways Apple fought to defend against.

Apple has yet to comment about the lawsuit.

Security flaws

On August 4, a report claimed that Apple's iCloud Private Relay was susceptible to a number of leaks in WebKit. Apple requires all browsers to use WebKit on iPhone, which means all mobile browsers for iOS are affected.

DNS prefetching, WebAuthn for Passkeys, and WebTransport can all reveal data about a user, even if they're using a proxy or iCloud Private Relay.

DNS prefetching in iOS 26 meant that hostnames could be resolved through the normal DNS path rather than through a proxy, exposing some data. WebAuthn's Passkey validation file revealed IP addresses, with WebTransport also doing so when opening a direct HTTP/3 connection.

While Apple will have to address all of the issues in due course, they will be elements that the new lawsuit will be leaning on.

items.title: Your iPhone can capture the Perseids meteor shower if you use the right tools
items.content_html:
The iPhone is a surprisingly capable meteor-hunting camera, but it's definitely not a point-and-shoot sort of situation. Here's how to take excellent photos of the Perseids, satellites, and more.

It's August, which means those in the northern hemisphere are being treated to the annual Perseids meteor shower. If you've got an iPhone, you're pretty much ready to go take some stunning astrophotography shots yourself.

Of course, it's not as simple as heading outside and pointing your iPhone at the sky, but you probably already knew that. Fortunately, we're here to help.

Don't expect perfection

While the iPhone can take incredible pictures, it's still a smartphone, not a full-featured DSLR. You're going to want to temper your expectations, especially if this is your first time using your iPhone for astrophotography.

It's going to take you some extra time, effort, and fiddling to find what works for you. And here's the kicker: there's no universal magic method for taking the best pictures.

You'll get different results based on whether you're using a Pro model or a standard iPhone. Typically, Pro-level phones, like the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, have larger sensors than their standard counterparts.

Similarly, there's going to be differences between an older iPhone, like the iPhone 14, and a newer iPhone.

But that doesn't mean you shouldn't try. A "just okay" picture is the first step to taking great pictures, and its certainly better than no pictures at all.

Still, I'd like to remind you of the important part here: don't forget to actually look up and enjoy the meteor shower. Spending the entire night trying to get the perfect picture isn't going to mean much if you don't enjoy your time out there.

So grab your iPhone, a cooler full of your favorite drinks, and a few friends or family members, and make a night of it.

The darker the better

If you're going to make an attempt to get some good pictures, you're going to need to find a location that has the lowest level of light pollution you can find. This seems obvious, but good locations tend to fill up quickly, especially for events like this.

Fortunately, in 2026, the height of the Perseids meteor shower and the new moon coincide. August 10 through August 14 should be ideal viewing in most locations that are decently away from cities.

If possible, try to find a rural location where you have permission to park your car if you're not lucky enough to have your own suitable property.

Non-negotiable: The humble tripod

Regardless of which iPhone you have, a tripod is non-optional. Night photography relies on long exposure times, so holding your phone while snapping a shot is a sure-fire way to ensure you'll ruin it.

Fortunately, they're also ridiculously cheap, and you can get a good one for a few bucks from Amazon.

Also ensure you've got a stable place to shoot, like the hood of a car, a patio table, or a flat piece of ground. If not, you might want to pick up a portable stool or drag along a spare cooler.

And while it's not strictly necessary, it's not a bad idea to have a remote shutter button. If you've got an Apple Watch, you already have one on hand.

If not, again, they're not terribly expensive to pick up. Alternatively, sometimes you can use a Bluetooth speaker's volume controls in a pinch — just make sure you test before you travel all the way to some remote location.

Get yourself NightCap

Astrophotography requires a camera to make the most of what little light there is. On traditional digital cameras, this is done by opening the shutter for longer exposure times and increasing the ISO to higher values.

Which is why you probably thought using your iPhone's built-in Night Mode would be sufficient. Unfortunately, it's not.

This is because instead of taking one long exposure, it rapidly shoots a burst of shorter images and stacks them together to boost brightness.

Night Mode works surprisingly well for photographing the aurora borealis | Image credit: Amber Neely

While this does great to, say, capture the Milky Way out in the desert, or even the Northern Lights in a sleepy little Western Pennsylvanian town, it's not a good solution for meteors. In fact, Night Mode won't capture those lovely trails at all.

Redditor nerdcan, for example, learned this the hard way after trying to photograph the Perseids with an iPhone using Night Mode. While the picture was stunning, it wasn't quit what they were looking for.

Image credit: Reddit user nerdcan

But that doesn't mean you don't have options.

NightCap Camera is a fan-favorite app that you can snag from the App Store that is designed for this exact scenario. Even better: it's a one-time $2.99 purchase.

NightCap has a dedicated Meteor Mode which sets everything up for you. It automatically takes about 720 photos per hour with a five-second exposure time.

If you're worried about your storage, don't be. NightCap only saves photos that it thinks contain a meteor.

Image credit: NightCap Team

However, because you're going to be taking so many photos, I suggest taking a portable battery pack with you, if possible. It's better than running out of battery in the busiest part of the night, after all.

Be prepared to edit

Once you get some good shots, don't be afraid to go edit them. You can do so with any number of apps, including the built-in Photos app.

If your picture looks a little washed out, try lowering your exposure. If the image is very dark, don't start by raising your exposure; this can introduce a lot of ugly noise into your image.

Instead, head over to your Highlights and boost them as needed. Sometimes raising your shadow levels can also help recover a bit more of your foreground detail.

Another helpful trick for any photography that might be lacking in contrast is boosting Contrast. You can overdo this, so start with less than you think and increase slowly — you can always come back if you need to.

Once you've completed those steps, try setting your Black Point again. Increase it until the sky gets dark once again, which should help to bring a bit more life back into the image.

If you find that your image is still a bit lackluster, try increasing both Definition and Sharpness. Again, you can easily overdo this.

Instead of cranking it to maximum, zoom into part of your image and increase slowly. The idea is to sharpen the edges of the stars and meteors without highlighting the noise itself.

Practice makes perfect

Ultimately, like everything else in life, practice makes perfect. And there's no better way to practice than to get outside and take the pictures yourself.

If you can, try not to limit yourself to just one night of stargazing while you're learning. The Perseids continue until August 24 and peak on August 12 and 13. You've got plenty of time to experiment!

attachments.title: Your iPhone can capture the Perseids meteor shower if you use the right tools

items.title: Discrimination lawsuit involving converted Jewish employee settled by Apple
items.content_html:
An Apple Genius was fired after failing to meet grooming standards, but the individual filed a lawsuit claiming religious discrimination. That lawsuit has now been settled by Apple for $150,000.

Apple is a large company with thousands of employees across retail, engineering, and corporate entities. It isn't immune from discrimination and the lawsuits that result.

According to a Law360 document read by 9to5Mac, Apple has agreed to settle a religious discrimination lawsuit. The company will pay out $150,000 and provide religious discrimination training, though there was no admission of wrongdoing in the settlement.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission filed the original lawsuit in September 2025 after an employee was fired. Apple said the employee was fired due to a lack of meeting grooming standards, but the employee alleged it was due to their asking off for Shabbat.

The Apple Genius had worked at the company for 16 years and had a reportedly good performance record. They converted to Judaism in 2023 and began asking to take off work from sunset on Friday to Saturday night to observe the religious practice of not working during Shabbat.

The employee was denied repeatedly, then grooming complaints started coming in. After a request to get a religious holiday off, the employee was terminated.

$80,000 of the settlement acts as backpay that will be taxed while $70,000 covers damages and interest. Apple has 30 days to issue the payments to the ex-employee.

attachments.title: Discrimination lawsuit involving converted Jewish employee settled by Apple

items.title: New in iOS 27 beta 5: 'Before Searching' settings, updated app icons, more
items.content_html:
Apple's fifth developer beta of iOS 27 has just arrived, and with it, redesigned icons for several key apps, and a lot more than normal than this late in the beta cycle. Here's what's new.

On Monday, three weeks after the release of iOS 27 beta 4, Apple made the fifth developer beta available for download. iOS 27 beta 1 introduced the long-overdue Siri AI, while the second beta included improvements to the Apple Home and Apple Wallet apps.

The third beta brought additional voice customization options for Siri AI, in the form of pace and expressivity sliders, albeit only for American English voices. Monday's iOS 27 developer beta, however, expands these settings to British English voices.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

Still, the new settings aren't available across all devices running iOS 27. Advanced Siri AI features require at least 12GB of RAM on iOS 27, hence the restriction, meaning the new voice sliders can only be found on an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, or iPhone Air.

As with most beta updates, visual tweaks are also present in iOS 27 beta 5. Icons for the Preview, Remote, Safari, Settings, and Siri applications have been updated, as has the Orders icon in the Apple Wallet app.

The Siri icon now features a more prominent Liquid Glass look, while the app icon for Safari now has a dot in the center. Apple has also included new update screens when the Apple Wallet, Apple Music, App Store, and Photos apps are launched for the first time.

iOS 27 beta 5 features a new 'Before Searching' option in the Settings app.

In the Settings app itself, under the Search Settings section, Apple has added a new option labeled Before Searching. This lets users choose how many apps appear as suggestions during searches, among other things.

Additionally, the Settings app now also shows when the most recent iOS update was installed. This detail could be useful for those who rely on automatic software updates.

Apple has also tweaked the Control Center with iOS 27 beta 5. Cellular network types are no longer displayed, so you won't see "5G" or "LTE" when your phone is connected to a Wi-Fi network. However, the Control Center and Status bar do feature new cellular icon bars.

Meanwhile, when a screenshot is taken on Monday's beta, the the annotations toolbar will now shrink and hover. It's a neat visual modification, but nothing groundbreaking.

Overall, the fifth developer beta of iOS 27 is a relatively light release. Aside from the updated app icons, Siri voice settings, and Before Search settings, the beta doesn't offer anything the average user would notice.

AppleInsider and Apple strongly advise against users installing test operating systems or beta software onto primary or "mission-critical" hardware. That warning stands for both developer betas and public beta builds.

More updates, more often

As noted before, Apple has said that users should expect these minor security updates to continue. The company will no longer delay including updates in upcoming scheduled releases.

AppleInsider, alongside Apple, suggests that you download the update as soon as it is available as a finalized release. These kinds of updates are critical for patching vulnerabilities and keeping your devices performing optimally.

items.title: Kuo pours water on rumor of $1B Apple chip stockpile at TSMC
items.content_html:
Market rumors claim TSMC is holding onto a billion-dollar stockpile of Apple chips due to not having enough memory to complete packaging. However, a prominent analyst doubts it to be the case.

The persisting memory supply crisis has caused problems with the supply chain, in both sourcing chips for products and in paying high prices for them too. While there is certainly a crisis at hand, not every major supply chain-related claim will be completely true.

On August 10, TF Securities analyst Ming-Chi Kuo wrote about market rumors that TSMC had a stockpile of 2-nanometer chips made for Apple. Valued at $1 billion, the pile was supposedly made of processor wafers for semi-finished products.

The apparent reason was due to a DRAM supply shortage, because Apple has memory attached to the System on Chip (SoC) for its Apple Silicon chips. Since there's not enough memory available, those chips couldn't be packaged.

Kuo adds that the apparent evidence for the claim was TSMC's Q2 2026 earnings call, which mentioned "increased inventory days" due to the ramp-up of production of 2-nanometer chips.

However, Kuo disagrees with the claims, because Apple and TSMC's working relationship involves intense planning. Something that couldn't realistically cause this to happen at all.

A doubtful stockpile

In discussing the rumor, Kuo admits that his industry research shows Apple's hardware shipments have been downgraded in 2026 due to memory shortages.

The key problem with the rumor is that Apple's processor orders with TSMC are planned about three months in advance. They're also based on the amount of memory available, meaning TSMC wouldn't be put into a position where it produces massive quantities of chips without the memory to go with it.

TSMC certainly can produce and stockpile half-made products in advance. But, since the bottleneck isn't TSMC, Kuo says Apple has "little reason" to pay TSMC to make the stockpile in the first place.

Memory supply is tight, Kuo adds, but he insists that he hasn't heard of any "dramatic development" like a billion-dollar chip stockpile that's awaiting more memory to arrive. "It's hard for such dramatic developments to occur," he states.

As for the call commentary as proof, Kuo points out that it couldn't be directly attributed to an Apple chip stockpile for a few reasons. Partly because TSMC's inventory includes finished goods, raw materials, supplies, and spare parts as well as semi-completed items.

TSMC also increases its "inventory days" in tandem with production ramp-ups for new advanced processes. This is not a phenomenon that's new to TSMC at all.

Lastly, TSMC isn't just supplying 2-nanometer chips to Apple. It also supplies to other firms, including AMD and MediaTek, meaning any such stockpiling would affect multiple companies.

Ultimately, while it is true that Apple is working to get around its memory issues by doing things like checking out politically problematic supply sources, it's not billion-dollar-stockpile bad.

Evidently, rumors aren't just limited to supposed specs and colors of iPhones.

attachments.title: Kuo pours water on rumor of $1B Apple chip stockpile at TSMC

items.title: Fifth developer betas of iOS 27, macOS 27 land as testing continues
items.content_html:
The fifth round of developer betas is here for iOS 27, iPadOS 27, tvOS 27, watchOS 27, visionOS 27, and macOS 27 as testing for the milestone releases rolls on.

Apple has reached the fifth round of developer betas for its upcoming fall releases. So far, the releases include the developer betas for iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, tvOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27.

The fifth appears after the fourth, which were distributed on July 20.

The third developer builds arrived on July 6, while the second occurred on June 22 for most of the operating systems. The watchOS 27 counterparts landed later, on June 23 and June 25.

The first developer builds of iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, tvOS 27, visionOS 27, and watchOS 27 were made available on June 8, right after the WWDC keynote.

The fifth builds are:

  • iOS 27 beta 5 is 24A5408d, replacing 24A5390f
  • iPadOS 27 beta 5 is 24A5408d, replacing 24A5390f
  • macOS 27 beta 5 is 26A5406e, replacing 26A5388g
  • tvOS 27 beta 5 is 24J5346a, replacing 24J5325d
  • watchOS 27 beta 5 is 24R5347a, replacing 24R5325h
  • visionOS 27 beta 5 is 24M5348b, replacing 24M5326g

The first round of changes included updates to Liquid Glass, the long-awaited overhaul of Siri, child-protective features, and many other smaller changes.

The second iOS 27 developer beta included an update to Apple TV in the Home app, showing it like a connected HomePod or HomePod mini. The Apple Wallet also added a new insights option, albeit in a non-functional fashion.

The third included some visual tweaks, with more customization options added for Siri AI on newer iPhone models.

At your own risk

While AppleInsider regularly warns readers that people trying out beta software should do so on secondary, spare hardware instead of their mission-critical or daily driver devices, it's something that actually matters more this time around.

It's because Apple's early developer betas are for an operating system that is still under active development. There's a higher chance of buggy, broken, and potentially harmful elements being distributed.

The initial builds are also intended to help developers learn about the operating system changes before the final public release later in 2026. It's not meant to be used by consumers.

Unless you have a vested interest in using them, such as app development, don't install the early developer betas.

Instead, members of the public should seek out the public betas. They are much safer alternatives if you want to try out iOS 27 now.

Even so, while the public betas reduce risk to your data compared to the developer betas, there is still some risk.

Find any changes in the new builds? Reach out to us on X at @AppleInsider or @Andrew_OSU, or send Andrew an email at andrew@AppleInsider.com.

items.title: Photo leak backs up massive iPhone 18 Pro Max battery rumor
items.content_html:
A photograph seems to back up claims of the increased battery capacity fo the iPhone 18 Pro Max, weighing in at a massive 5,391mAh.

One month away from the introduction of the iPhone 18 Pro range, and the photographic leaks are starting to roll in. In the latest one to surface, it seems the earlier claims of a super-sized iPhone 18 Pro Max battery may be true.

Shots shared to Naver by Yeuz1122 show what appears to be an Apple battery from multiple angles. The accompanying post explains that the battery is for the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

The battery is shown with the Apple logo and regulatory text, including a small printed section near the connector. Shots show the front and back, as well as the top section.

The leaker adds that the battery capacity is labeled as 5,391mAh, which appears in the regulatory text section. This is the same capacity as listed for the U.S. version of the iPhone 18 Pro Max in a July 6 leak.

As the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max approaches, it is worth remembering that the quantity of leaks will intensify. There's no guarantee that any of the details are genuine, even images and video in this AI-centric world, and the only real confirmation will happen at launch.

items.title: Jefferies cuts AAPL target to $263.66, downgrades to Underperform
items.content_html:
Analyst firm Jefferies has downgraded Apple stock to underperform alongside a price cut, because the firm believes Apple has cancelled its all-glass design for the still-unannounced iPhone 20.

Apple has a lot going on to be concerned about. RAM pricing will just get worse, SSD flash cells are a year away from relief, and so forth. One firm thinks that they have a bigger problem than all that.

Analyst Edison Lee of Jefferies is concerned that the iPhone 20 will not be an all-glass device.

"The all-glass iPhone has been cancelled due to low yield," Lee said. "We view this as a major setback to efforts to bring in higher-priced iPhones amid soaring memory costs."

Lee believed that this all-glass body would be migrated to the iPhone Pro and iPhone Pro Max models eventually. This would, in turn, raise their selling price and margin.

So now, the analyst is troubled that the folding iPhone will be niche at over $2000. Furthermore, he says that it is the "only key driver of higher ASP and margin."

The firm is relying on "supply chain checks." Glass supply chain checks have never been a reliable indicator of Apple's future plans for product releases. Apple's glass production is easier to secure and hide, given that most of it is inside the US.

Also, finalization of the glass does not have to happen this early. Even with a radical new all-glass enclosure, which was always only rumored for the iPhone 20 with low certainty, Apple can take until February of release year to lock down the design.

Most of the rumors for the iPhone 20 have said that the device will be more like the iPhone Air, than the all-glass enclosure that's been rumored and patented for over a decade.

Wall Street mostly disagrees with bearish Jefferies

Jefferies is bucking the trend of the rest of Wall Street. The firm is one of three that have Apple at an Underperform rating. The firm remains notably underwater on Apple stock, and has not had a price target above what Apple's actual stock price has been for years.

As CNBC notes on Monday, of the 47 firms that cover Apple, 10 have a strong buy rating, 20 have a buy, 14 have a hold and now three have that underperform. Zero have a sell rating.

The current price of the stock is $310.00 before trading opens on August 10, and was $313.33 at close on Friday. The after-hours drop was gradual over the weekend, and the last few times Jefferies had a note like this, it didn't impact the market at all.

The highest price target is $400, and the consensus average is $319.48, including Jefferies. We've asked for the note in full.

items.title: Guide to Apple Intelligence using Qwen briefly appears for Apple users in China
items.content_html:
Apple Support in China has published detailed instructions on how local Mac users can utilize Alibaba's Qwen AI with Siri, but the guide was quickly removed.

Back in March 2026, Apple Intelligence was finally launched and available in China, except it wasn't. Apple had released it seemingly accidentally, and certainly without approval from the Chinese government, so it was rapidly pulled.

Now Apple has done a similar thing with a support document. As first noted by Reuters, Apple Support in China published a guide for Mac users on connecting Qwen to get Writing Tools and Siri working with it. There was no equivalent guide for the iPhone or iPad.

Presumably there will be, but as local Chinese sources including news aggregator ReadHub have subsequently reported, the Mac guide is gone. When asked about it, Apple Support reportedly would not comment on the guide having been released.

"We are notified in advance whenever a feature or new project is launched," Apple Support is reported to have said (in translation). "We have not received any such notification, and the feature integrating Apple Intelligence with Qianwen [aka Qwen] has not yet been released in mainland China."

China has extremely complex laws regarding the release of AI features, and to all practical purposes requires firms like Apple to partner with local companies. Apple is working with both Alibaba and Baidu.

Recently, the Chinese government has allowed Apple Intelligence to be officially registered for use on iPhones in the region. It's not clear what steps remain before users can have Apple Intelligence, but it is still coming.

attachments.title: Guide to Apple Intelligence using Qwen briefly appears for Apple users in China
